case_info.scenario: A 70-year-old man presented to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of a pruritic exanthem that began on his scalp and face and spread across most of his body over a 2-month period. The patient had no fever, night sweats, fatigue, recent unintentional weight loss, shortness of breath, chest pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. He reported no new prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements prior to the onset of the exanthem. He had no history of psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, or other skin disorder, and no recent viral or bacterial infection. On presentation, his temperature was 37.1 °C (98.7 °F); blood pressure, 128/86 mm Hg; heart rate, 110/min; and respiratory rate, 30/min. Physical examination revealed confluent salmon-colored plaques composed of folliculocentric scaly papules across his body with several patches of unaffected skin on his trunk. The patient had waxy, exfoliative scale on the volar aspect of his hands and feet and thickened, onycholytic nails. Severe ectropion prevented complete eyelid closure (Figure). He was referred to the emergency department, where laboratory testing revealed a normal complete blood cell count and normal lactate dehydrogenase level. The patient was admitted to the hospital and was treated with intravenous fluids and daily wet-wrap therapy with topical triamcinolone ointment (0.1%) applied to his trunk, arms, and legs, followed by a layer of warm, damp gauze and dry, cotton pajamas.

case_info.caption: Clinical examination at the time of presentation revealed generalized and coalescing salmon-colored plaques with “islands of sparing” on the abdomen (far left); waxy, exfoliative scale on the palms (center left) and soles (center right); and ectropion (far right).
case_info.explanation: B. Obtain skin biopsy with T-cell clonality studies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that generalized salmon-colored plaques with areas of unaffected skin (“islands of sparing”) and waxy palmoplantar keratoderma are characteristic of pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP).1Testing for myositis-specific autoantibodies (choice A), anti-dsDNA (choice C), and HLA-B27 (choice D) is incorrect because the patient’s skin findings were not typical of dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or reactive arthritis, respectively. Erythroderma, also known as exfoliative dermatitis, is diffuse dermal erythema and scaling involving more than 90% of the body surface area.1Erythroderma is a dermatologic emergency because it may cause excessive loss of fluid and heat, which can lead to hypothermia and rigors, dehydration, hypotension, and high-output cardiac failure.2Due to disruption of the skin barrier, erythroderma is also associated with increased risk of cellulitis. Erythroderma is most commonly associated with psoriasis or atopic dermatitis but can occur in patients with infections (eg, HIV, scabies), malignancy (eg, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma), medications (eg, antibiotics, anticonvulsants), and congenital skin diseases.1 PRP is a rare, inflammatory disorder that may cause erythroderma, especially in adults.3Of the 6 clinical subtypes of PRP, type I (classic adult) is the most common, accounting for 55% of cases.3,4Patients with type I PRP have waxy palmoplantar keratoderma and salmon-colored plaques with sharply-demarcated areas of spared skin that typically start on the upper half of the body and spread downward. Hyperkeratotic nail changes, nonscarring hair loss, and ectropion are also common findings in type I PRP.3,4The other PRP subtypes are type II (atypical adult), type III (classical juvenile), type IV (circumscribed juvenile), type V (atypical juvenile), and type VI (HIV-related).3 PRP affects males and females of all ages, and incidence peaks in children at age 1 to 10 years and in adults at age 50 to 60 years.3,4The US Health and Human Services Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center estimates that fewer than 5000 people in the US currently have PRP.5Although the pathophysiology of PRP is unknown, some cases may be precipitated by bacterial or viral infections.3Some patients with PRP type V have an autosomal dominantly–acquired or sporadic genetic variant of caspase recruitment domain family, member 14 (CARD14), which is an activator of a signaling pathway involved in inflammation.3,4 The differential diagnosis of erythrodermic PRP includes psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, generalized hypersensitivity reactions, immunobullous diseases, acquired ichthyoses, and erythrokeratoderma variabilis.4The diagnosis of PRP is made based on clinical findings and histopathological characteristics on skin biopsy.3,4T-cell clonality studies should be obtained for patients with erythroderma and ectropion and/or palmoplantar keratoderma to evaluate for Sezary syndrome, a distinctive form of erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with leukemic involvement of malignant T cells. The prognosis of PRP varies among subtypes.1 Although no evidence-based guidelines exist for treatment of PRP, common treatments include topical corticosteroids, methotrexate, systemic retinoids, phototherapy, and cyclosporine.3,4,6Improvement or resolution of PRP has been reported with use of biologic therapies (such as tumor necrosis factor inhibitors and anti–IL-17 or anti–IL-12/IL-23 biologics) in case reports and small case series.3,7-9 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s upper back revealed acanthosis with broad rete ridges, confluent hypergranulosis, and alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, consistent with the diagnosis of PRP. Flow cytometry and T-cell clonality studies did not reveal findings characteristic of Sezary syndrome, and results of HIV testing were negative. During his hospitalization, the patient was treated with acitretin (50 mg daily), methotrexate (25 mg weekly), infliximab (10 mg/kg every 4 weeks), and topical triamcinolone ointment (0.1%). Six months later, his erythroderma had resolved, and he underwent oculoplastic surgery for repair of his ectropion. At his most recent clinic visit, 3 years after initial presentation, the patient was taking infliximab (5 mg/kg every 6 weeks) and methotrexate (12.5 mg weekly), and findings on skin examination were normal.

The biopsy with T-cell clonality studies remains important but should follow this hematologic assessment.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:

[Important rules]

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain skin biopsy with T-cell clonality studies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that generalized salmon-colored plaques with areas of unaffected skin (“islands of sparing”) and waxy palmoplantar keratoderma are characteristic of pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP).1Testing for myositis-specific autoantibodies (choice A), anti-dsDNA (choice C), and HLA-B27 (choice D) is incorrect because the patient’s skin findings were not typical of dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or reactive arthritis, respectively. Erythroderma, also known as exfoliative dermatitis, is diffuse dermal erythema and scaling involving more than 90% of the body surface area.1Erythroderma is a dermatologic emergency because it may cause excessive loss of fluid and heat, which can lead to hypothermia and rigors, dehydration, hypotension, and high-output cardiac failure.2Due to disruption of the skin barrier, erythroderma is also associated with increased risk of cellulitis. Erythroderma is most commonly associated with psoriasis or atopic dermatitis but can occur in patients with infections (eg, HIV, scabies), malignancy (eg, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma), medications (eg, antibiotics, anticonvulsants), and congenital skin diseases.1 PRP is a rare, inflammatory disorder that may cause erythroderma, especially in adults.3Of the 6 clinical subtypes of PRP, type I (classic adult) is the most common, accounting for 55% of cases.3,4Patients with type I PRP have waxy palmoplantar keratoderma and salmon-colored plaques with sharply-demarcated areas of spared skin that typically start on the upper half of the body and spread downward. Hyperkeratotic nail changes, nonscarring hair loss, and ectropion are also common findings in type I PRP.3,4The other PRP subtypes are type II (atypical adult), type III (classical juvenile), type IV (circumscribed juvenile), type V (atypical juvenile), and type VI (HIV-related).3 PRP affects males and females of all ages, and incidence peaks in children at age 1 to 10 years and in adults at age 50 to 60 years.3,4The US Health and Human Services Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center estimates that fewer than 5000 people in the US currently have PRP.5Although the pathophysiology of PRP is unknown, some cases may be precipitated by bacterial or viral infections.3Some patients with PRP type V have an autosomal dominantly–acquired or sporadic genetic variant of caspase recruitment domain family, member 14 (CARD14), which is an activator of a signaling pathway involved in inflammation.3,4 The differential diagnosis of erythrodermic PRP includes psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, generalized hypersensitivity reactions, immunobullous diseases, acquired ichthyoses, and erythrokeratoderma variabilis.4The diagnosis of PRP is made based on clinical findings and histopathological characteristics on skin biopsy.3,4T-cell clonality studies should be obtained for patients with erythroderma and ectropion and/or palmoplantar keratoderma to evaluate for Sezary syndrome, a distinctive form of erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with leukemic involvement of malignant T cells. The prognosis of PRP varies among subtypes.1 Although no evidence-based guidelines exist for treatment of PRP, common treatments include topical corticosteroids, methotrexate, systemic retinoids, phototherapy, and cyclosporine.3,4,6Improvement or resolution of PRP has been reported with use of biologic therapies (such as tumor necrosis factor inhibitors and anti–IL-17 or anti–IL-12/IL-23 biologics) in case reports and small case series.3,7-9 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s upper back revealed acanthosis with broad rete ridges, confluent hypergranulosis, and alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, consistent with the diagnosis of PRP. Flow cytometry and T-cell clonality studies did not reveal findings characteristic of Sezary syndrome, and results of HIV testing were negative. During his hospitalization, the patient was treated with acitretin (50 mg daily), methotrexate (25 mg weekly), infliximab (10 mg/kg every 4 weeks), and topical triamcinolone ointment (0.1%). Six months later, his erythroderma had resolved, and he underwent oculoplastic surgery for repair of his ectropion. At his most recent clinic visit, 3 years after initial presentation, the patient was taking infliximab (5 mg/kg every 6 weeks) and methotrexate (12.5 mg weekly), and findings on skin examination were normal.

     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more

   Definition:

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain skin biopsy with T-cell clonality studies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that generalized salmon-colored plaques with areas of unaffected skin (“islands of sparing”) and waxy palmoplantar keratoderma are characteristic of pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP).1Testing for myositis-specific autoantibodies (choice A), anti-dsDNA (choice C), and HLA-B27 (choice D) is incorrect because the patient’s skin findings were not typical of dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or reactive arthritis, respectively. Erythroderma, also known as exfoliative dermatitis, is diffuse dermal erythema and scaling involving more than 90% of the body surface area.1Erythroderma is a dermatologic emergency because it may cause excessive loss of fluid and heat, which can lead to hypothermia and rigors, dehydration, hypotension, and high-output cardiac failure.2Due to disruption of the skin barrier, erythroderma is also associated with increased risk of cellulitis. Erythroderma is most commonly associated with psoriasis or atopic dermatitis but can occur in patients with infections (eg, HIV, scabies), malignancy (eg, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma), medications (eg, antibiotics, anticonvulsants), and congenital skin diseases.1 PRP is a rare, inflammatory disorder that may cause erythroderma, especially in adults.3Of the 6 clinical subtypes of PRP, type I (classic adult) is the most common, accounting for 55% of cases.3,4Patients with type I PRP have waxy palmoplantar keratoderma and salmon-colored plaques with sharply-demarcated areas of spared skin that typically start on the upper half of the body and spread downward. Hyperkeratotic nail changes, nonscarring hair loss, and ectropion are also common findings in type I PRP.3,4The other PRP subtypes are type II (atypical adult), type III (classical juvenile), type IV (circumscribed juvenile), type V (atypical juvenile), and type VI (HIV-related).3 PRP affects males and females of all ages, and incidence peaks in children at age 1 to 10 years and in adults at age 50 to 60 years.3,4The US Health and Human Services Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center estimates that fewer than 5000 people in the US currently have PRP.5Although the pathophysiology of PRP is unknown, some cases may be precipitated by bacterial or viral infections.3Some patients with PRP type V have an autosomal dominantly–acquired or sporadic genetic variant of caspase recruitment domain family, member 14 (CARD14), which is an activator of a signaling pathway involved in inflammation.3,4 The differential diagnosis of erythrodermic PRP includes psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, generalized hypersensitivity reactions, immunobullous diseases, acquired ichthyoses, and erythrokeratoderma variabilis.4The diagnosis of PRP is made based on clinical findings and histopathological characteristics on skin biopsy.3,4T-cell clonality studies should be obtained for patients with erythroderma and ectropion and/or palmoplantar keratoderma to evaluate for Sezary syndrome, a distinctive form of erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with leukemic involvement of malignant T cells. The prognosis of PRP varies among subtypes.1 Although no evidence-based guidelines exist for treatment of PRP, common treatments include topical corticosteroids, methotrexate, systemic retinoids, phototherapy, and cyclosporine.3,4,6Improvement or resolution of PRP has been reported with use of biologic therapies (such as tumor necrosis factor inhibitors and anti–IL-17 or anti–IL-12/IL-23 biologics) in case reports and small case series.3,7-9 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s upper back revealed acanthosis with broad rete ridges, confluent hypergranulosis, and alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, consistent with the diagnosis of PRP. Flow cytometry and T-cell clonality studies did not reveal findings characteristic of Sezary syndrome, and results of HIV testing were negative. During his hospitalization, the patient was treated with acitretin (50 mg daily), methotrexate (25 mg weekly), infliximab (10 mg/kg every 4 weeks), and topical triamcinolone ointment (0.1%). Six months later, his erythroderma had resolved, and he underwent oculoplastic surgery for repair of his ectropion. At his most recent clinic visit, 3 years after initial presentation, the patient was taking infliximab (5 mg/kg every 6 weeks) and methotrexate (12.5 mg weekly), and findings on skin examination were normal.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Clinical examination at the time of presentation revealed generalized and coalescing salmon-colored plaques with “islands of sparing” on the abdomen (far left); waxy, exfoliative scale on the palms (center left) and soles (center right); and ectropion (far right).
case_info.explanation: B. Obtain skin biopsy with T-cell clonality studies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that generalized salmon-colored plaques with areas of unaffected skin (“islands of sparing”) and waxy palmoplantar keratoderma are characteristic of pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP).1Testing for myositis-specific autoantibodies (choice A), anti-dsDNA (choice C), and HLA-B27 (choice D) is incorrect because the patient’s skin findings were not typical of dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or reactive arthritis, respectively. Erythroderma, also known as exfoliative dermatitis, is diffuse dermal erythema and scaling involving more than 90% of the body surface area.1Erythroderma is a dermatologic emergency because it may cause excessive loss of fluid and heat, which can lead to hypothermia and rigors, dehydration, hypotension, and high-output cardiac failure.2Due to disruption of the skin barrier, erythroderma is also associated with increased risk of cellulitis. Erythroderma is most commonly associated with psoriasis or atopic dermatitis but can occur in patients with infections (eg, HIV, scabies), malignancy (eg, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma), medications (eg, antibiotics, anticonvulsants), and congenital skin diseases.1 PRP is a rare, inflammatory disorder that may cause erythroderma, especially in adults.3Of the 6 clinical subtypes of PRP, type I (classic adult) is the most common, accounting for 55% of cases.3,4Patients with type I PRP have waxy palmoplantar keratoderma and salmon-colored plaques with sharply-demarcated areas of spared skin that typically start on the upper half of the body and spread downward. Hyperkeratotic nail changes, nonscarring hair loss, and ectropion are also common findings in type I PRP.3,4The other PRP subtypes are type II (atypical adult), type III (classical juvenile), type IV (circumscribed juvenile), type V (atypical juvenile), and type VI (HIV-related).3 PRP affects males and females of all ages, and incidence peaks in children at age 1 to 10 years and in adults at age 50 to 60 years.3,4The US Health and Human Services Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center estimates that fewer than 5000 people in the US currently have PRP.5Although the pathophysiology of PRP is unknown, some cases may be precipitated by bacterial or viral infections.3Some patients with PRP type V have an autosomal dominantly–acquired or sporadic genetic variant of caspase recruitment domain family, member 14 (CARD14), which is an activator of a signaling pathway involved in inflammation.3,4 The differential diagnosis of erythrodermic PRP includes psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, generalized hypersensitivity reactions, immunobullous diseases, acquired ichthyoses, and erythrokeratoderma variabilis.4The diagnosis of PRP is made based on clinical findings and histopathological characteristics on skin biopsy.3,4T-cell clonality studies should be obtained for patients with erythroderma and ectropion and/or palmoplantar keratoderma to evaluate for Sezary syndrome, a distinctive form of erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with leukemic involvement of malignant T cells. The prognosis of PRP varies among subtypes.1 Although no evidence-based guidelines exist for treatment of PRP, common treatments include topical corticosteroids, methotrexate, systemic retinoids, phototherapy, and cyclosporine.3,4,6Improvement or resolution of PRP has been reported with use of biologic therapies (such as tumor necrosis factor inhibitors and anti–IL-17 or anti–IL-12/IL-23 biologics) in case reports and small case series.3,7-9 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s upper back revealed acanthosis with broad rete ridges, confluent hypergranulosis, and alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, consistent with the diagnosis of PRP. Flow cytometry and T-cell clonality studies did not reveal findings characteristic of Sezary syndrome, and results of HIV testing were negative. During his hospitalization, the patient was treated with acitretin (50 mg daily), methotrexate (25 mg weekly), infliximab (10 mg/kg every 4 weeks), and topical triamcinolone ointment (0.1%). Six months later, his erythroderma had resolved, and he underwent oculoplastic surgery for repair of his ectropion. At his most recent clinic visit, 3 years after initial presentation, the patient was taking infliximab (5 mg/kg every 6 weeks) and methotrexate (12.5 mg weekly), and findings on skin examination were normal.

  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain skin biopsy with T-cell clonality studies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that generalized salmon-colored plaques with areas of unaffected skin (“islands of sparing”) and waxy palmoplantar keratoderma are characteristic of pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP).1Testing for myositis-specific autoantibodies (choice A), anti-dsDNA (choice C), and HLA-B27 (choice D) is incorrect because the patient’s skin findings were not typical of dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or reactive arthritis, respectively. Erythroderma, also known as exfoliative dermatitis, is diffuse dermal erythema and scaling involving more than 90% of the body surface area.1Erythroderma is a dermatologic emergency because it may cause excessive loss of fluid and heat, which can lead to hypothermia and rigors, dehydration, hypotension, and high-output cardiac failure.2Due to disruption of the skin barrier, erythroderma is also associated with increased risk of cellulitis. Erythroderma is most commonly associated with psoriasis or atopic dermatitis but can occur in patients with infections (eg, HIV, scabies), malignancy (eg, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma), medications (eg, antibiotics, anticonvulsants), and congenital skin diseases.1 PRP is a rare, inflammatory disorder that may cause erythroderma, especially in adults.3Of the 6 clinical subtypes of PRP, type I (classic adult) is the most common, accounting for 55% of cases.3,4Patients with type I PRP have waxy palmoplantar keratoderma and salmon-colored plaques with sharply-demarcated areas of spared skin that typically start on the upper half of the body and spread downward. Hyperkeratotic nail changes, nonscarring hair loss, and ectropion are also common findings in type I PRP.3,4The other PRP subtypes are type II (atypical adult), type III (classical juvenile), type IV (circumscribed juvenile), type V (atypical juvenile), and type VI (HIV-related).3 PRP affects males and females of all ages, and incidence peaks in children at age 1 to 10 years and in adults at age 50 to 60 years.3,4The US Health and Human Services Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center estimates that fewer than 5000 people in the US currently have PRP.5Although the pathophysiology of PRP is unknown, some cases may be precipitated by bacterial or viral infections.3Some patients with PRP type V have an autosomal dominantly–acquired or sporadic genetic variant of caspase recruitment domain family, member 14 (CARD14), which is an activator of a signaling pathway involved in inflammation.3,4 The differential diagnosis of erythrodermic PRP includes psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, generalized hypersensitivity reactions, immunobullous diseases, acquired ichthyoses, and erythrokeratoderma variabilis.4The diagnosis of PRP is made based on clinical findings and histopathological characteristics on skin biopsy.3,4T-cell clonality studies should be obtained for patients with erythroderma and ectropion and/or palmoplantar keratoderma to evaluate for Sezary syndrome, a distinctive form of erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with leukemic involvement of malignant T cells. The prognosis of PRP varies among subtypes.1 Although no evidence-based guidelines exist for treatment of PRP, common treatments include topical corticosteroids, methotrexate, systemic retinoids, phototherapy, and cyclosporine.3,4,6Improvement or resolution of PRP has been reported with use of biologic therapies (such as tumor necrosis factor inhibitors and anti–IL-17 or anti–IL-12/IL-23 biologics) in case reports and small case series.3,7-9 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s upper back revealed acanthosis with broad rete ridges, confluent hypergranulosis, and alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, consistent with the diagnosis of PRP. Flow cytometry and T-cell clonality studies did not reveal findings characteristic of Sezary syndrome, and results of HIV testing were negative. During his hospitalization, the patient was treated with acitretin (50 mg daily), methotrexate (25 mg weekly), infliximab (10 mg/kg every 4 weeks), and topical triamcinolone ointment (0.1%). Six months later, his erythroderma had resolved, and he underwent oculoplastic surgery for repair of his ectropion. At his most recent clinic visit, 3 years after initial presentation, the patient was taking infliximab (5 mg/kg every 6 weeks) and methotrexate (12.5 mg weekly), and findings on skin examination were normal.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain skin biopsy with T-cell clonality studies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that generalized salmon-colored plaques with areas of unaffected skin (“islands of sparing”) and waxy palmoplantar keratoderma are characteristic of pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP).1Testing for myositis-specific autoantibodies (choice A), anti-dsDNA (choice C), and HLA-B27 (choice D) is incorrect because the patient’s skin findings were not typical of dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or reactive arthritis, respectively. Erythroderma, also known as exfoliative dermatitis, is diffuse dermal erythema and scaling involving more than 90% of the body surface area.1Erythroderma is a dermatologic emergency because it may cause excessive loss of fluid and heat, which can lead to hypothermia and rigors, dehydration, hypotension, and high-output cardiac failure.2Due to disruption of the skin barrier, erythroderma is also associated with increased risk of cellulitis. Erythroderma is most commonly associated with psoriasis or atopic dermatitis but can occur in patients with infections (eg, HIV, scabies), malignancy (eg, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma), medications (eg, antibiotics, anticonvulsants), and congenital skin diseases.1 PRP is a rare, inflammatory disorder that may cause erythroderma, especially in adults.3Of the 6 clinical subtypes of PRP, type I (classic adult) is the most common, accounting for 55% of cases.3,4Patients with type I PRP have waxy palmoplantar keratoderma and salmon-colored plaques with sharply-demarcated areas of spared skin that typically start on the upper half of the body and spread downward. Hyperkeratotic nail changes, nonscarring hair loss, and ectropion are also common findings in type I PRP.3,4The other PRP subtypes are type II (atypical adult), type III (classical juvenile), type IV (circumscribed juvenile), type V (atypical juvenile), and type VI (HIV-related).3 PRP affects males and females of all ages, and incidence peaks in children at age 1 to 10 years and in adults at age 50 to 60 years.3,4The US Health and Human Services Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center estimates that fewer than 5000 people in the US currently have PRP.5Although the pathophysiology of PRP is unknown, some cases may be precipitated by bacterial or viral infections.3Some patients with PRP type V have an autosomal dominantly–acquired or sporadic genetic variant of caspase recruitment domain family, member 14 (CARD14), which is an activator of a signaling pathway involved in inflammation.3,4 The differential diagnosis of erythrodermic PRP includes psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, generalized hypersensitivity reactions, immunobullous diseases, acquired ichthyoses, and erythrokeratoderma variabilis.4The diagnosis of PRP is made based on clinical findings and histopathological characteristics on skin biopsy.3,4T-cell clonality studies should be obtained for patients with erythroderma and ectropion and/or palmoplantar keratoderma to evaluate for Sezary syndrome, a distinctive form of erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with leukemic involvement of malignant T cells. The prognosis of PRP varies among subtypes.1 Although no evidence-based guidelines exist for treatment of PRP, common treatments include topical corticosteroids, methotrexate, systemic retinoids, phototherapy, and cyclosporine.3,4,6Improvement or resolution of PRP has been reported with use of biologic therapies (such as tumor necrosis factor inhibitors and anti–IL-17 or anti–IL-12/IL-23 biologics) in case reports and small case series.3,7-9 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s upper back revealed acanthosis with broad rete ridges, confluent hypergranulosis, and alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, consistent with the diagnosis of PRP. Flow cytometry and T-cell clonality studies did not reveal findings characteristic of Sezary syndrome, and results of HIV testing were negative. During his hospitalization, the patient was treated with acitretin (50 mg daily), methotrexate (25 mg weekly), infliximab (10 mg/kg every 4 weeks), and topical triamcinolone ointment (0.1%). Six months later, his erythroderma had resolved, and he underwent oculoplastic surgery for repair of his ectropion. At his most recent clinic visit, 3 years after initial presentation, the patient was taking infliximab (5 mg/kg every 6 weeks) and methotrexate (12.5 mg weekly), and findings on skin examination were normal.

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain skin biopsy with T-cell clonality studies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that generalized salmon-colored plaques with areas of unaffected skin (“islands of sparing”) and waxy palmoplantar keratoderma are characteristic of pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP).1Testing for myositis-specific autoantibodies (choice A), anti-dsDNA (choice C), and HLA-B27 (choice D) is incorrect because the patient’s skin findings were not typical of dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or reactive arthritis, respectively. Erythroderma, also known as exfoliative dermatitis, is diffuse dermal erythema and scaling involving more than 90% of the body surface area.1Erythroderma is a dermatologic emergency because it may cause excessive loss of fluid and heat, which can lead to hypothermia and rigors, dehydration, hypotension, and high-output cardiac failure.2Due to disruption of the skin barrier, erythroderma is also associated with increased risk of cellulitis. Erythroderma is most commonly associated with psoriasis or atopic dermatitis but can occur in patients with infections (eg, HIV, scabies), malignancy (eg, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma), medications (eg, antibiotics, anticonvulsants), and congenital skin diseases.1 PRP is a rare, inflammatory disorder that may cause erythroderma, especially in adults.3Of the 6 clinical subtypes of PRP, type I (classic adult) is the most common, accounting for 55% of cases.3,4Patients with type I PRP have waxy palmoplantar keratoderma and salmon-colored plaques with sharply-demarcated areas of spared skin that typically start on the upper half of the body and spread downward. Hyperkeratotic nail changes, nonscarring hair loss, and ectropion are also common findings in type I PRP.3,4The other PRP subtypes are type II (atypical adult), type III (classical juvenile), type IV (circumscribed juvenile), type V (atypical juvenile), and type VI (HIV-related).3 PRP affects males and females of all ages, and incidence peaks in children at age 1 to 10 years and in adults at age 50 to 60 years.3,4The US Health and Human Services Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center estimates that fewer than 5000 people in the US currently have PRP.5Although the pathophysiology of PRP is unknown, some cases may be precipitated by bacterial or viral infections.3Some patients with PRP type V have an autosomal dominantly–acquired or sporadic genetic variant of caspase recruitment domain family, member 14 (CARD14), which is an activator of a signaling pathway involved in inflammation.3,4 The differential diagnosis of erythrodermic PRP includes psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, generalized hypersensitivity reactions, immunobullous diseases, acquired ichthyoses, and erythrokeratoderma variabilis.4The diagnosis of PRP is made based on clinical findings and histopathological characteristics on skin biopsy.3,4T-cell clonality studies should be obtained for patients with erythroderma and ectropion and/or palmoplantar keratoderma to evaluate for Sezary syndrome, a distinctive form of erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with leukemic involvement of malignant T cells. The prognosis of PRP varies among subtypes.1 Although no evidence-based guidelines exist for treatment of PRP, common treatments include topical corticosteroids, methotrexate, systemic retinoids, phototherapy, and cyclosporine.3,4,6Improvement or resolution of PRP has been reported with use of biologic therapies (such as tumor necrosis factor inhibitors and anti–IL-17 or anti–IL-12/IL-23 biologics) in case reports and small case series.3,7-9 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s upper back revealed acanthosis with broad rete ridges, confluent hypergranulosis, and alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, consistent with the diagnosis of PRP. Flow cytometry and T-cell clonality studies did not reveal findings characteristic of Sezary syndrome, and results of HIV testing were negative. During his hospitalization, the patient was treated with acitretin (50 mg daily), methotrexate (25 mg weekly), infliximab (10 mg/kg every 4 weeks), and topical triamcinolone ointment (0.1%). Six months later, his erythroderma had resolved, and he underwent oculoplastic surgery for repair of his ectropion. At his most recent clinic visit, 3 years after initial presentation, the patient was taking infliximab (5 mg/kg every 6 weeks) and methotrexate (12.5 mg weekly), and findings on skin examination were normal.

case_info.explanation: B. Obtain skin biopsy with T-cell clonality studies The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that generalized salmon-colored plaques with areas of unaffected skin (“islands of sparing”) and waxy palmoplantar keratoderma are characteristic of pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP).1Testing for myositis-specific autoantibodies (choice A), anti-dsDNA (choice C), and HLA-B27 (choice D) is incorrect because the patient’s skin findings were not typical of dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or reactive arthritis, respectively. Erythroderma, also known as exfoliative dermatitis, is diffuse dermal erythema and scaling involving more than 90% of the body surface area.1Erythroderma is a dermatologic emergency because it may cause excessive loss of fluid and heat, which can lead to hypothermia and rigors, dehydration, hypotension, and high-output cardiac failure.2Due to disruption of the skin barrier, erythroderma is also associated with increased risk of cellulitis. Erythroderma is most commonly associated with psoriasis or atopic dermatitis but can occur in patients with infections (eg, HIV, scabies), malignancy (eg, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma), medications (eg, antibiotics, anticonvulsants), and congenital skin diseases.1 PRP is a rare, inflammatory disorder that may cause erythroderma, especially in adults.3Of the 6 clinical subtypes of PRP, type I (classic adult) is the most common, accounting for 55% of cases.3,4Patients with type I PRP have waxy palmoplantar keratoderma and salmon-colored plaques with sharply-demarcated areas of spared skin that typically start on the upper half of the body and spread downward. Hyperkeratotic nail changes, nonscarring hair loss, and ectropion are also common findings in type I PRP.3,4The other PRP subtypes are type II (atypical adult), type III (classical juvenile), type IV (circumscribed juvenile), type V (atypical juvenile), and type VI (HIV-related).3 PRP affects males and females of all ages, and incidence peaks in children at age 1 to 10 years and in adults at age 50 to 60 years.3,4The US Health and Human Services Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center estimates that fewer than 5000 people in the US currently have PRP.5Although the pathophysiology of PRP is unknown, some cases may be precipitated by bacterial or viral infections.3Some patients with PRP type V have an autosomal dominantly–acquired or sporadic genetic variant of caspase recruitment domain family, member 14 (CARD14), which is an activator of a signaling pathway involved in inflammation.3,4 The differential diagnosis of erythrodermic PRP includes psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, generalized hypersensitivity reactions, immunobullous diseases, acquired ichthyoses, and erythrokeratoderma variabilis.4The diagnosis of PRP is made based on clinical findings and histopathological characteristics on skin biopsy.3,4T-cell clonality studies should be obtained for patients with erythroderma and ectropion and/or palmoplantar keratoderma to evaluate for Sezary syndrome, a distinctive form of erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with leukemic involvement of malignant T cells. The prognosis of PRP varies among subtypes.1 Although no evidence-based guidelines exist for treatment of PRP, common treatments include topical corticosteroids, methotrexate, systemic retinoids, phototherapy, and cyclosporine.3,4,6Improvement or resolution of PRP has been reported with use of biologic therapies (such as tumor necrosis factor inhibitors and anti–IL-17 or anti–IL-12/IL-23 biologics) in case reports and small case series.3,7-9 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s upper back revealed acanthosis with broad rete ridges, confluent hypergranulosis, and alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, consistent with the diagnosis of PRP. Flow cytometry and T-cell clonality studies did not reveal findings characteristic of Sezary syndrome, and results of HIV testing were negative. During his hospitalization, the patient was treated with acitretin (50 mg daily), methotrexate (25 mg weekly), infliximab (10 mg/kg every 4 weeks), and topical triamcinolone ointment (0.1%). Six months later, his erythroderma had resolved, and he underwent oculoplastic surgery for repair of his ectropion. At his most recent clinic visit, 3 years after initial presentation, the patient was taking infliximab (5 mg/kg every 6 weeks) and methotrexate (12.5 mg weekly), and findings on skin examination were normal.
